# Project Charter

## Testing Standards

- Lightweight but SOC 2-ready. The bar is "tests where they earn their keep,
integration tests where the contract crosses a boundary."

- Go core: `go test ./... -race` must pass on every PR. Target ≥80% line
  coverage on `core/` packages (blob, bundle, event, llm, mcp, scheduler,
  session, memory, config). Table-driven tests preferred.
- Black-box integration tests required for: bundle resolver, LLM adapter
  layer (each provider), MCP pool lifecycle, scheduler missed-run catch-up,
  and append-only event log invariants.
- Frontend: Vitest unit tests for non-trivial composables and store logic;
  `vue-tsc --noEmit` must be clean. E2E (Playwright) deferred until the
  RPC surface stabilizes.
- No mocking of the event log in tests that assert audit/replay behavior —
  use a real on-disk log under a temp dir.
- TDD is encouraged but not mandatory; security-sensitive code paths
  (credential redaction, bundle integrity verification, sandbox boundaries)
  MUST land with tests in the same commit.


## Quality Gates

- - Go: `gofmt`, `goimports`, `go vet`, and `golangci-lint run` must be clean.
- Frontend: `eslint` and `prettier --check` must be clean; `vue-tsc`
  must report zero errors.
- `wails build` must succeed for the host platform on every PR.
- Pre-commit hooks are recommended but not enforced; CI is the source of
  truth.
- Conventional Commits required for commit messages; commits must be
  attributed (signed-off or signed) per DIRECTIVE_029.
- No `git add .` / `git add -A` in agent or human workflows — staging is
  explicit per DIRECTIVE_033, both for hygiene and to avoid accidental
  secret inclusion.


## Performance Benchmarks

- - Cold runtime startup (Wails app first window): under 2 seconds on a
  modern laptop.
- RPC roundtrip for non-LLM calls: under 50 ms p99 local.
- Bundle resolution from lockfile (typical bundle set): under 500 ms.
- Event log append: under 5 ms p99 local.
- Scheduler missed-run reconciliation on resume: under 1 second for the
  first 100 catch-up jobs.
- These are targets to defend against regression, not premature
  optimization budgets — measure before tuning.


## Branch Strategy

- - `main` is protected. No direct pushes to `main` under any circumstance,
  including hotfixes — open a PR with a `fix/` branch.
- All changes ship via pull request. Minimum one (1) approving review
  from a maintainer before merge.
- Branch naming: `feat/<slug>`, `fix/<slug>`, `chore/<slug>`,
  `docs/<slug>`, `refactor/<slug>`, `charter/<slug>`.
- Squash-merge by default; merge commits allowed only for charter or
  release branches.
- PRs must reference the spec/mission they implement when one exists
  (DIRECTIVE_010).
- Material architectural decisions land with an ADR (DIRECTIVE_003).

- Deployment constraints: - Local-first. The core runtime MUST function with zero network access
  except when explicitly invoking a remote model adapter.
- The RPC surface used by the Wails app is the same contract a future
  hosted backend will expose — backend swaps stay behind interfaces in
  `core/`. No leaking Wails-specific types into `core/`.
- Distribution targets: signed macOS (notarized), Linux (AppImage / deb),
  Windows (msi/exe) builds via Wails.
- Two-track release: open-source core (license follows Sigil) and a
  commercial enterprise build that adds enterprise-only modules behind
  build tags or separate binaries — never by forking core.
- Versioning: SemVer once the public Go API and bundle format reach v1.
  Until then, breaking changes allowed but called out in CHANGELOG.

## Policy Summary

- Intent: kaneaz-harness is a model-agnostic, configuration-first AI harness and
context management system for agentic workflows. Skills, MCP servers, agent
definitions, hooks, and context files (AGENT.md and friends) are declared
as composable, versioned bundles — the way you ship a Helm chart or Brew
formula. A team bundle pins shared conventions and tools; a personal
overlay layers on top; the runtime resolves the dependency graph
reproducibly from a lockfile. Bundles run against any model — Anthropic,
OpenAI, local Ollama — through a uniform adapter layer, so configuration is
the durable artifact and the model is a swappable input.

Every agent run is recorded as an append-only event log, making replay,
branching, audit, and "what context did the model actually see" first-class.
Sessions can be scheduled on cron with missed runs catching up when the
laptop reopens — no always-on server required.

The runtime ships today as a Go library wrapped by a native Wails app,
behind the same RPC surface a hosted backend would later expose, so
multi-device sync and cloud execution become additive features rather than
a rewrite. Two-track distribution: an open-source core (license follows the
parent Sigil project) and a commercial enterprise build. Operating
principles: local-first, security-first, lightweight by default — never
force users to take on more configuration or ceremony than they need.

- Languages/Frameworks: - Go 1.23+ for the core runtime, RPC surface, and library API
  (module: github.com/sigil-tech/kaneaz-harness)
- Wails v2 for the native desktop shell (macOS / Linux / Windows)
- Vue 3 + Vite for the frontend; vue-tsc for type checking
- Bundle format authored as YAML/TOML with lockfile-based pinning
- Adapter layer integrates Anthropic, OpenAI, and Ollama SDKs;
  additional providers are added by implementing the adapter interface,
  not by patching core
- MCP integration via the standard Model Context Protocol

- Testing: Lightweight but SOC 2-ready. The bar is "tests where they earn their keep,

## Project Directives

1. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_001` to planning and implementation decisions.
2. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_003` to planning and implementation decisions.
3. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_010` to planning and implementation decisions.
4. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_024` to planning and implementation decisions.
5. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_028` to planning and implementation decisions.
6. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_029` to planning and implementation decisions.
7. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_030` to planning and implementation decisions.
8. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_033` to planning and implementation decisions.
9. Apply doctrine directive `DIRECTIVE_036` to planning and implementation decisions.
10. Respect risk boundaries: Security-first and SOC 2-ready posture. The harness handles model
credentials, user prompts, and an auditable event log — these must be
treated as sensitive by default.

- No secrets, API keys, model credentials, or sample user data committed
  to the repository at any time. Pre-commit secret scanning is recommended.
- Local-first invariant: prompts, contexts, and event logs MUST NOT leave
  the device without explicit user opt-in.
- Bundle integrity: lockfile hashes are verified before resolution. No
  remote-code-execution surface in the resolver — bundles declare
  configuration, not arbitrary code execution paths.
- LLM adapter layer redacts known credential patterns from event log
  payloads by default; redaction rules are configurable but never
  disable-able to "off" without an explicit, persisted user override.
- MCP server execution runs with least-privilege; no implicit elevation,
  no shared filesystem access beyond declared bundle scopes.
- Append-only event log: immutability is a hard invariant. Log entries
  are never edited or deleted in place — corrections are new entries that
  reference the prior entry.
- Commit attribution per DIRECTIVE_029 supports SOC 2 audit trails for
  who changed what and when.
- Architectural integrity (DIRECTIVE_001): the layered boundary
  `frontend → rpc → core` is enforced; `core/` does not import Wails or
  frontend packages.

11. Keep documentation synchronized with workflow and behavior changes.

| `PARADIGM:c4-incremental-detail-modeling` | paradigm | Architecture communication through progressive zoom -- from the broadest system landscape down to individual components -- so that each audience sees the right level of detail without drowning in irrelevance. Inspired by Simon Brown's C4 model, the approach defines four hierarchical abstraction levels (Software System, Container, Component, Code) and a small set of supporting diagram types (System Landscape, Dynamic, Deployment). Each level answers a different question for a different stakeholder: Level 1 (Context) shows actors and boundaries for business sponsors; Level 2 (Containers) shows deployable units and technology choices for architects and DevOps; Level 3 (Components) shows logical structure for developers; Level 4 (Code) shows implementation detail only when automated generation makes it cheap. The paradigm is notation- independent and tooling-independent -- Mermaid, PlantUML, Structurizr, or whiteboard sketches all qualify, provided every diagram carries a title, a legend, labelled elements with descriptions, and labelled unidirectional relationships. The guiding heuristic: produce only the levels that add value and keep each diagram reviewable in under five minutes.

## Amendment Process

- Charter changes ship as a PR on a `charter/<slug>` branch.
- The PR edits `.kittify/charter/charter.md` (the authoritative source).
  Do NOT hand-edit `governance.yaml` or `directives.yaml` — they are
  regenerated by `spec-kitty charter sync`.
- At least one maintainer approval required, same as code PRs.
- Material policy changes (testing thresholds, security boundaries,
  branch protection, license posture) require an accompanying ADR under
  `docs/adr/`.
- On merge, the next workflow action will pick up the new governance
  context automatically via `spec-kitty charter context`.


## Exception Policy

- One-off exceptions to a directive are allowed when justified, and MUST
  be documented either in an inline ADR or in the commit body, citing
  the directive ID being deviated from and the reason.
- Exceptions to security-related directives (credential handling, bundle
  integrity, event-log immutability, no-direct-push-to-main) require
  maintainer sign-off in the PR review, not just a justification note.
- If the same exception is requested more than twice, the charter is
  amended instead — recurring exceptions indicate the rule is wrong, not
  that the situation is special.
